passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it introduces equitable principles into a body of law that has historically demanded the strict satisfaction of formal requirements. At common law, a promise is enforceable only when supported by consideration — that is, when something of legal value is exchanged between the parties. Promissory estoppel, however, allows a court to enforce a promise even in the absence of consideration, provided that the promisee has relied on the promise to her detriment and that it would be inequitable to allow the promisor to resile from what was said. The tension between these two approaches has generated considerable doctrinal instability, and courts applying promissory estoppel have not consistently identified either the conditions under which the doctrine operates or the remedy it is meant to afford.

The difficulty begins with the threshold requirement of reliance. Most courts agree that the promisee's reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable — that is, the promisor must have known, or should have known, that the promisee would act upon the promise. But courts have diverged sharply on the question of how substantial that reliance must be. Some jurisdictions require that the promisee demonstrate a significant change in position, such as the abandonment of a business opportunity or the expenditure of a large sum. Others have found detrimental reliance satisfied by comparatively modest acts, such as declining to seek an alternative arrangement. This divergence produces markedly different outcomes in cases that are otherwise substantially similar. Consider, for example, two decisions issued in the early 1990s in different American states involving employers who made oral assurances of long-term employment to candidates who had already resigned from existing positions. In one state, the court held that resignation alone was insufficient reliance; in the other, identical facts supported a successful estoppel claim. This inconsistency is difficult to justify and reflects not a principled distinction but rather the varying tolerance of different courts for departures from the consideration requirement.

Equally contested is the matter of remedy. At common law, a successful plaintiff recovers expectation damages — the benefit of the bargain — whereas promissory estoppel, rooted in equity, would seem to call for reliance damages, which restore the plaintiff to the position she held before acting on the promise. Yet courts have not uniformly confined promissory estoppel to reliance recovery. Several influential decisions in the latter half of the twentieth century awarded the plaintiff the full expectation measure, effectively treating the equitable doctrine as functionally equivalent to contract enforcement. Whether this extension is faithful to the doctrine's equitable foundations is doubtful, and it seems to conflate what are properly distinct remedial regimes. Courts that award expectation damages through the vehicle of promissory estoppel do little more than relabel contract enforcement in the language of equity, obscuring the doctrinal rationale for the remedy they grant. One may hope that a clearer articulation of when reliance recovery, rather than expectation recovery, is appropriate will eventually emerge from appellate courts willing to examine the doctrine with greater conceptual rigor.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be eliminated from common law jurisdictions because it undermines the consideration requirement that gives contracts their binding force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been applied inconsistently by courts with respect to both the threshold reliance requirement and the appropriate remedy, reflecting deeper doctrinal instability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in the early 1990s issued contradictory rulings on employment estoppel claims, demonstrating that oral assurances of employment are unreliable bases for legal action.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel and contract law are best understood as two versions of the same doctrine, since both ultimately protect the expectation interests of promisees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Appellate courts should award reliance damages rather than expectation damages in all promissory estoppel cases in order to restore the doctrine's equitable foundations.

explanations.correct: The passage's thesis — stated in paragraph 1 and developed in paragraphs 2 and 3 — is that promissory estoppel is applied inconsistently on two fronts: the reliance threshold and the remedy. B captures this dual instability across the full passage.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — the author critiques inconsistency but never advocates eliminating the doctrine.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates both strands of the argument (reliance threshold and remedy) that span paragraphs 2 and 3.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the employment cases are an illustrative example in paragraph 2, not the main point of the passage.
explanations.D: This inverts the author's concern; the author explicitly rejects conflating estoppel with contract enforcement.
explanations.E: This is the author's closing suggestion, not the main point — a classic 'restates the closing recommendation as the thesis' trap.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward courts that award expectation damages through the vehicle of promissory estoppel can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: cautious approval, because such awards produce outcomes that are fair to promisees who have genuinely relied on promises to their detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured indifference, because the choice between reliance and expectation damages has no practical effect on the plaintiff's recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical skepticism, because such courts obscure the doctrinal rationale for the remedy they grant by conflating distinct remedial regimes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: strong condemnation, because awarding expectation damages through estoppel constitutes a fundamental violation of equitable principles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: tentative acceptance, because although the practice departs from equity, it may help courts resolve the inconsistency surrounding the reliance threshold.

explanations.correct: The author states that awarding expectation damages through promissory estoppel is 'doubtful,' 'conflates what are properly distinct remedial regimes,' and 'does little more than relabel contract enforcement' — language that signals critical skepticism without rising to outright condemnation.
explanations.A: The author does not approve of this practice; the passage characterizes it as doctrinal confusion.
explanations.B: The author clearly does not view this as a matter of indifference — the passage expresses concern about the doctrinal obscuration it produces.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Doubtful,' 'conflates,' and 'obscuring' signal critical skepticism at the right intensity.
explanations.D: Overstated — the author uses measured language ('doubtful,' 'seems to conflate'), not the strong condemnation that 'fundamental violation' implies.
explanations.E: The author never suggests the practice helps resolve the reliance threshold inconsistency; this is an unsupported rationalization.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and situated within a broader tension; the inconsistency in its application is then examined on two distinct dimensions; and the passage closes with a critical assessment and an expression of hope for future clarification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing theories of contract law are described; a series of court decisions is analyzed to determine which theory is superior; and the passage concludes by endorsing one theory over the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problematic court decision is introduced; its historical precedents are traced across several jurisdictions; and a statutory remedy is proposed as a solution to the inconsistency it generated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; its origins in Roman law are described; its subsequent transformation in Anglo-American courts is traced; and the passage ends by noting its current obsolescence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The requirements of a legal doctrine are set out in detail; a single landmark case is analyzed at length; and the passage argues that the case was wrongly decided and should be overturned.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its tension with consideration doctrine. Paragraph 2 examines inconsistency in the reliance threshold. Paragraph 3 examines inconsistency in remedies and closes with the author's critique and hope for appellate clarification. A captures all three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Correct. This accurately describes all three paragraphs' functions.
explanations.B: The passage does not pit two theories against each other to select a winner; it critiques internal inconsistency within one doctrine.
explanations.C: No single problematic decision is the focus; no statutory remedy is proposed.
explanations.D: No Roman law origins are discussed, and the doctrine is not described as obsolete.
explanations.E: The passage discusses multiple cases, not a single landmark; it does not argue any case should be overturned.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition that most courts agree must be satisfied for the doctrine of promissory estoppel to apply?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee must have suffered a financial loss that exceeds the value of the original promise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisor must have reduced the promise to writing and signed it before a witness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisee's reliance on the promise must have been reasonable and foreseeable by the promisor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promise must have been made in a commercial rather than a personal or social context.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must have provided something of legal value in exchange for the promisor's assurance.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly: 'Most courts agree that the promisee's reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable — that is, the promisor must have known, or should have known, that the promisee would act upon the promise.' C paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: The passage does not state any financial-loss-exceeds-promise-value threshold; this is not mentioned.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly notes that promissory estoppel can apply to oral assurances; a writing requirement is not stated.
explanations.C: Correct. This is stated in paragraph 2 as a point of consensus.
explanations.D: The passage discusses employment contexts but never restricts the doctrine to commercial settings.
explanations.E: This describes the consideration requirement, which the passage notes promissory estoppel operates without — directly the opposite of what is asked.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plaintiff who prevails on a promissory estoppel claim should generally recover only enough to restore her to the position she occupied before relying on the promise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be abolished in common law jurisdictions, since promissory estoppel demonstrates that enforceable promises need not be supported by an exchange of value.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts that have awarded expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases have done so because they carefully weighed the equitable foundations of the doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral assurances of long-term employment should never form the basis of a promissory estoppel claim, since employment relationships require written documentation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a variant of contract law that has gradually absorbed all of contract law's remedial principles.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that promissory estoppel, 'rooted in equity, would seem to call for reliance damages, which restore the plaintiff to the position she held before acting on the promise.' The author then criticizes courts that award expectation damages instead, strongly implying endorsement of reliance recovery as the proper default. A mirrors this inference.
explanations.A: Correct. The author's characterization of reliance damages as the equity-consistent remedy, combined with criticism of expectation awards, supports this inference.
explanations.B: The author critiques inconsistency in promissory estoppel but never advocates abolishing consideration; this overreaches.
explanations.C: The author states the opposite — that such courts obscure the doctrinal rationale rather than carefully weighing equitable foundations.
explanations.D: The employment cases are used as illustrations of inconsistency; the author never says oral assurances categorically cannot support an estoppel claim.
explanations.E: The author explicitly rejects this conflation, arguing that extending expectation damages through estoppel 'conflates what are properly distinct remedial regimes.'

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the two early-1990s employment cases (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that the reliance threshold in promissory estoppel is applied inconsistently across jurisdictions, producing different outcomes from materially identical facts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that oral assurances of employment are never a reliable basis for a promissory estoppel claim in any American jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce the broader historical development of promissory estoppel within the American common law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide evidence that expectation damages, rather than reliance damages, are the appropriate remedy in employment estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the doctrine of promissory estoppel should be codified in statutory form to resolve jurisdictional inconsistency.

explanations.correct: The cases are introduced with 'Consider, for example' and directly follow the author's claim that divergence in the reliance threshold 'produces markedly different outcomes in cases that are otherwise substantially similar.' They function to concretely illustrate that general claim. A accurately captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: Correct. The cases are a specific illustration of the inconsistency already asserted in the paragraph.
explanations.B: The cases show inconsistency, not a universal rule against oral assurances; one state's court actually upheld the estoppel claim.
explanations.C: The cases are not introduced to provide historical background but to exemplify a specific doctrinal problem.
explanations.D: Remedies are not discussed in paragraph 2; the cases concern the reliance threshold, not the damages question.
explanations.E: No statutory codification is proposed anywhere in the passage; this is a plausible-but-unused rhetorical move.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that courts awarding expectation damages through promissory estoppel are conflating two distinct remedial regimes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several legal historians have argued that the distinction between law and equity was largely abolished in most common law jurisdictions during the nineteenth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In practice, promisees who have detrimentally relied on a promise frequently suffer losses that are equal in value to the benefit of the bargain they expected to receive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some jurisdictions that recognize promissory estoppel have enacted statutes requiring courts to apply the doctrine only to written promises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A series of appellate decisions in the late twentieth century expressly analyzed the equitable foundations of promissory estoppel before awarding expectation damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal scholars have proposed that promissory estoppel be replaced by a statutory cause of action modeled on the civilian doctrine of culpa in contrahendo.

explanations.correct: The author's claim rests on the premise that law and equity operate as distinct regimes with distinct remedial logics. If the law/equity distinction was substantively abolished — making contract law and equitable doctrines part of the same unified regime — then awarding expectation damages through estoppel would not constitute a conflation of two distinct systems, thereby undermining the author's critique. A directly attacks this foundational premise.
explanations.A: Correct. If law and equity are no longer distinct regimes, the author's charge of 'conflation' loses its doctrinal foundation.
explanations.B: Even if reliance losses happened to equal expectation losses in practice, this would not justify the legal rationale for awarding expectation damages through an equitable doctrine; it addresses magnitude, not the doctrinal basis the author criticizes.
explanations.C: This concerns a writing requirement, which is unrelated to the remedy debate the author raises; it does not bear on the conflation claim.
explanations.D: Courts that analyzed equitable foundations before awarding expectation damages might show thoughtfulness, but would not demonstrate that expectation and reliance damages are part of the same regime — they would still be awarding a measure the author argues is doctrinal misfit.
explanations.E: A proposal to replace the doctrine with a civilian analogue is irrelevant to whether current courts are conflating two regimes in existing common law.
